verses.text: When David and his men had come to Ziklag on the third day, the Amalekites had made a raid on the South, and on Ziklag, and had struck Ziklag, and burned it with fire,
and had taken captive the women and all who were in it, both small and great. They didn’t kill any, but carried them off, and went their way.
When David and his men came to the city, behold, it was burned with fire; and their wives, their sons, and their daughters were taken captive.
Then David and the people who were with him lifted up their voice and wept until they had no more power to weep.
David’s two wives were taken captive, Ahinoam the Jezreelitess, and Abigail the wife of Nabal the Carmelite.

David was greatly distressed; for the people spoke of stoning him, because the souls of all the people were grieved, every man for his sons and for his daughters; but David strengthened himself in Yahweh his God.
David said to Abiathar the priest, the son of Ahimelech, “Please bring the ephod here to me.” Abiathar brought the ephod to David.
David inquired of Yahweh, saying, “If I pursue after this troop, will I overtake them?” He answered him, “Pursue; for you will surely overtake them, and will without fail recover all.”
So David went, he and the six hundred men who were with him, and came to the brook Besor, where those who were left behind stayed.
But David pursued, he and four hundred men; for two hundred stayed behind, who were so faint that they couldn’t go over the brook Besor.
They found an Egyptian in the field, and brought him to David, and gave him bread, and he ate; and they gave him water to drink.
They gave him a piece of a cake of figs, and two clusters of raisins. When he had eaten, his spirit came again to him; for he had eaten no bread, and drank no water for three days and three nights.
David asked him, “To whom do you belong? Where are you from?” He said, “I am a young man of Egypt, servant to an Amalekite; and my master left me, because three days ago I got sick.
We made a raid on the South of the Cherethites, and on that which belongs to Judah, and on the South of Caleb; and we burned Ziklag with fire.”

David said to him, “Will you bring me down to this troop?” He said, “Swear to me by God that you will not kill me and not deliver me up into the hands of my master, and I will bring you down to this troop.”

When he had brought him down, behold, they were spread around over all the ground, eating, drinking, and dancing, because of all the great plunder that they had taken out of the land of the Philistines, and out of the land of Judah.
David struck them from the twilight even to the evening of the next day. Not a man of them escaped from there, except four hundred young men, who rode on camels and fled.
David recovered all that the Amalekites had taken; and David rescued his two wives.
There was nothing lacking to them, neither small nor great, neither sons nor daughters, neither plunder, nor anything that they had taken to them. David brought back all.
David took all the flocks and the herds, which they drove before those other livestock, and said, “This is David’s plunder.”

David came to the two hundred men, who were so faint that they could not follow David, whom also they had made to stay at the brook Besor; and they went out to meet David, and to meet the people who were with him. When David came near to the people, he greeted them.

Then all the wicked men and base fellows, of those who went with David, answered and said, “Because they didn’t go with us, we will not give them anything of the plunder that we have recovered, except to every man his wife and his children, that he may lead them away, and depart.”
Then David said, “Do not do so, my brothers, with that which Yahweh has given to us, who has preserved us, and delivered the troop that came against us into our hand.
Who will listen to you in this matter? For as his share is who goes down to the battle, so shall his share be who stays with the baggage. They shall share alike.”
It was so from that day forward, that he made it a statute and an ordinance for Israel to this day.
When David came to Ziklag, he sent some of the plunder to the elders of Judah, even to his friends, saying, “Behold, a present for you from the plunder of Yahweh’s enemies.”
He sent it to those who were in Bethel, to those who were in Ramoth of the South, to those who were in Jattir,
to those who were in Aroer, to those who were in Siphmoth, to those who were in Eshtemoa,
to those who were in Racal, to those who were in the cities of the Jerahmeelites, to those who were in the cities of the Kenites,
to those who were in Hormah, to those who were in Borashan, to those who were in Athach,
to those who were in Hebron, and to all the places where David himself and his men used to stay.

footnotes.content: Homecoming can shatter your heart. David arrived at Ziklag expecting shelter and found only ash. Yet sometimes the hardest moments teach us to stop looking for safety in places and begin to look for it in God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Amalekites took families captive instead of killing them—a terrible distinction, but a mercy wrapped in grief. When life seems stolen, we often don't see at first that we are not abandoned; we are still loved and pursued.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The city burned, wives and children gone—David's own family lost in the raid. He had to face the weight of loss not as a king but as a broken man, and it was there, in that breaking, that he learned to seek God's face.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His men wept until they had no more strength. Sometimes the grace of God meets us not in quick fixes but in being allowed to grieve fully, honestly, without shame. There is holiness in a man willing to cry.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Two wives lost—Ahinoam and Abigail, whom he had learned to love. The heart breaks for its own, and God does not ask us to pretend otherwise. But He also makes a way through the valley where we thought no way existed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His own men spoke of stoning him. In despair, they turned their grief into blame and aimed it at their leader. Yet David did what few do in such moments—he did not defend himself or flee, but 'strengthened himself in Yahweh his God.' That is the difference between a man and a leader.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David asked for the ephod, seeking God's direction through the priest. In his darkest hour, he did not run to weapons first or rage first—he sought counsel from heaven. That choice, before any action, changes everything.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God answered David clearly: pursue and you will recover all. Sometimes the Lord does not ask us to accept loss in silence; He calls us to fight for what He has given us. Faith and courage are not opposites.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David and six hundred men came to the brook Besor. Even in the midst of their own sorrow, they had gathered and stood ready. A leader's steadiness in grief can steady a whole people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Two hundred men stayed behind, too weary to continue. David did not shame them or leave them abandoned—they waited, and we learn later that the merciful act of staying would matter. Sometimes faithfulness is not dramatic.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They found an Egyptian servant abandoned in the field, hungry and alone. In their own extremity, David's men gave him bread and water. The poor and displaced have a claim on the hearts of those who follow Jesus.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three days without food or water—the man was as good as dead until David's men rescued him. Revival often comes through a simple gift given in kindness by ordinary people. We underestimate how much strength a piece of bread can restore.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The servant was abandoned by his master when sickness came. How quickly loyalty evaporates when you become a burden. Yet this rejected servant was about to become David's guide—God saw his worth when no one else did.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Egyptian revealed the Amalekite route: they had raided the South—Cherethites, Judah, Caleb's land, and Ziklag. Each place a home, each name a face. The scope of the raid became clear, and so did the scale of what must be recovered.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Egyptian asked for a covenant: don't kill me, don't hand me over. He needed to know he was safe with his rescuer. God's promise to us is that same covenant—we are rescued, and we are safe, held by His faithfulness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Amalekites feasted on their plunder, dancing and drinking, unguarded. They believed themselves victorious and secure. But those who live by theft sleep poorly, and their joy is hollow.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David struck them from twilight to evening—a full day and night of pursuit and battle. Only four hundred escaped on camels. The Lord gave the victory and the recovery, complete and overwhelming.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David recovered everything and rescued his wives. The promise God made came to pass—nothing lost, none forgotten. When the Lord restores, He restores with abundance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Nothing lacking—sons, daughters, plunder, and all. The text emphasizes the totality of recovery. God is not a God of partial restoration; He reclaims the whole person, the whole family, the whole future.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David claimed the plunder and declared it his. But a king's wealth is not merely possession; it is stewardship. What follows will show how he understood that better than most.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The two hundred who stayed at the brook came out to greet David and his men. They had not fought, yet they hoped. David greeted them—a simple word that carried forgiveness and welcome.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The able-bodied men spoke of dividing the plunder only among those who fought, leaving wives and children without. Exhaustion and greed conspired to make them cruel. In their victory, they forgot mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David said, 'Do not do so, my brothers.' He did not rebuke them harshly but called them brothers and reminded them of the Lord's preservation. A wise leader speaks to men's better nature first.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in David's principle: those who keep the supplies and tend the camp share equally with those who fight. In Jesus' Kingdom, the last shall be first, and a cup of water given to the least is honored as if given to Him. The Lord sees every faithful work.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This statute became law in Israel from that day forward. One man's mercy in a moment of victory became a principle that shaped a nation. A single act of justice, rooted in God's character, reaches forward into generations.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David sent gifts to the elders of Judah and his friends from the plunder. Having been restored, he gave generously. A grateful heart cannot help but bless those around it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Bethel, Ramoth, Jattir—the list of towns begins. Each name represents a place where David had found refuge, hospitality, or hope. His gifts were not abstract; they honored the kindness he had received.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Aroer, Siphmoth, Eshtemoa—the towns of the South. Each gift was a seed of loyalty and gratitude, planted where David had walked and been sustained.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Racal, Jerahmeelite cities, Kenite cities—even those outside Judah proper received his remembrance. A man who does not forget the small kindnesses of the past is a man worth following.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hormah, Borashan, Athach—the list lengthens. David's gifts mapped the geography of his loneliness and his grace; every refuge received acknowledgment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hebron and all the places where he and his men had stayed. The list closed with the places of his wandering. A man who remembers those who sheltered him in exile is one who understands that gratitude and honor are not burdens but treasures.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
